speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: We have capitalised on our geographical position and our strong adherence to the rule of law, to grow these services.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: In international arbitration, we have a comprehensive legal infrastructure that supports and at the same time intensively promotes arbitration alongside a robust and effective legal system.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: We have enhanced our laws, to constantly improve our system and to best meet the needs of the end user.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: We have a first class judiciary that is supportive of arbitration as a dispute resolution mechanism and these are amongst the main reasons why Singapore is the most preferred seat of arbitration in the world today.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: We have come far, in the last 25 years, since the Singapore International Arbitration Centre, the SIAC, was set up.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Today, Singapore is a popular seat for arbitration and also recognised as the third most preferred in international arbitration in the world.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: It is also the third most preferred arbitral institution, the SIAC, globally.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: This growth has only been possible with the close partnership between the Government and the legal fraternity.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: We share a common understanding about the value of alternative dispute resolution to Singapore's position as a legal services hub.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: At the same time, the arbitration landscape is constantly evolvingand we must be ever alert to changing needs and continue to improve Singapore's value propositions as a hub for international commercial arbitration.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: With the uncertainties facing the global economy, it is now even more important that we regularly review and enhance our legislation, so as to continue to build on our reputation for being a trusted and neutral jurisdiction, under-girded by a strong rule of law and a legal framework that is responsive and remains relevant to the users' evolving needs.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: This Bill, Mr Speaker, is moved in that spirit.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: In 2019, MinLaw conducted a broad public consultation on a number of proposals to improve and enhance and to consider for amendment of the International Arbitration Act or IAA.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: These proposals were aimed at enhancing our offerings, in the international arbitration arena and they included: the introduction of a default mode of appointment of arbitrators in multi-party situations; recognising that an arbitral tribunal and the High Court ought to have powers to enforce obligations of confidentiality; allowing a party to the arbitral proceedings to appeal to the High Court on a question of law arising out of an award, provided that parties have agreed to opt into this mechanism; and allowing parties to waive or limit the annulment grounds under the Model Law or the IAA.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: These are amongst the several proposals that were considered in the consultation in 2019.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: And received feedback from arbitral institutions, from professional bodies, from practitioners, from academics, from multi-national companies who are themselves users of the arbitration in the international arena, key industry experts, both local and foreign.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: We have studied the feedback and the views very carefully.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: We received a broad range of views, because this really represents the end-users and the market.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: We received views on whether to implement them and if so, how then these changes ought to be implemented.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Second, it recognises that the tribunal and the High Court have the power to enforce confidentiality obligations in an arbitration.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: The rest of the proposals which were considered in the public consultation are still being studied and evaluated by my Ministry.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: I wish to thank and place on record our gratitide to all those who have contributed their views, their time and suggestions.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: They have been very welcomed and most helpful in shaping our views.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: At present, the IAA provides a procedure for default appointment of arbitrators only where there are only two parties to a dispute; and where these parties have adopted an ad hoc arbitration instead of institutional arbitration or have chosen not to apply institutional arbitration rules.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: There is currently no similar procedure in the IAA or the UNCITRAL Model Law on International Commercial Arbitration, for arbitrations where the dispute involves more than two parties.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: As Members know, today as transactions become more complex, disputes become more complex, multi-party arbitrations have been a growing trend.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: It is no longer often that we see a case where there is a single claimant with a single respondent.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: The increasingly complex and diverse nature of contracts means that more often than not, these disputes will be multi-party in nature.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Where there are multiple parties, they may not be able to collectively agree on an arbitrator.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Indeed, it is sometimes not in their interest to do so.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: A group of claimants will probably find it easier to be aligned, but in some multi-party cases, the interests of the disputing parties are not necessarily aligned neatly into two opposing sides and very often, they are not.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: As a result, it is not easy for these two groups of parties to agree on who they wish to nominate as their respective arbitrator.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Such situations could also occur in disputes arising from multi-shareholder or multi-joint venture party disputes.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: In one example that was cited to us, the dispute comprised a state, a ministry and joint venture vehicle as the respondent.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: On the side of the claimants was a consortium of oil companies.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: The claimants were more easily able to co-ordinate and appoint an arbitrator, but when it came to the respondents, it was a lot more difficult as the different parties comprising the respondent group, comprised different entities with divergent interests.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: This would result in one side not having the benefit of a party appointed member on the tribunal, through no fault of his except that its interests were not coincident with the rest of the respondent group.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Other examples include claims by a developer against two contractors, in a situation where each of the contractors might have had a distinct role and each of the contractors might well have a reason for suggesting that the other contractor is at fault.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: In those situations, you would not expect the respondent parties to be coincident or aligned in terms of their choice of arbitrators.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: It is also not uncommon for respondents to try to delay or frustrate an arbitration by either failing to appoint an arbitrator or dragging their feet or just not taking part in the proceedings for nomination at all.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: These examples are just some, but they demonstrate the importance of having clear rules or procedures, upfront, to help parties to quickly resolve their differences, at the procedural stage.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: This is not a problem where parties have decided on a set of institutional rules, but it does become critical in the context of multi-party ad hoc arbitration situations where there is no agreed mechanism for the constitution of the arbitral tribunal, and where the parties' inability to agree on the appointment of their arbitrators would invariably lead to disagreement and delays in commencing the proceedings.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: This invariably adds to costs and unnecessary time spent on process and procedure, when the parties really ought to get into the heart of the substance of the dispute and resolve those disputes.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: The claimant must first appoint an arbitrator on or before the date of its request for arbitration.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: If there is more than one claimant, then all the claimants should make the appointment by agreement.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: The claimant or claimants must then inform the respondents of the appointment and state the appointed arbitrator together with the notice of arbitration.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: The respondent must then appoint an arbitrator after the receipt of the request for arbitration.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Again, if there is more than one respondent, all the respondents need to make or agree to the appointment.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: The respondent must inform the claimant or claimants of the appointment.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: In doing so, the appointing authority is required to have regard to and I quote, "all relevant circumstances".

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: So, a broad discretion, to consider all the facts, all the matters which arise in the context of that appointment exercise is to be considered. 9B(2) also allows for the appointing authority to consider the choices already made by the parties at that stage, if any, and at what stage the proceedings might be at.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: In doing so, the appointing authority may have regard to all relevant circumstances as I have mentioned and that authority may reappoint or may revoke any appointment that has already been made.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: The appointing authority may also designate any one of the three arbitrators as the presiding arbitrator.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: This process seeks to strike a balance between party autonomy and equality in the arbitration process.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: And this process is itself aligned with the rules of leading arbitral institutions on the multi-party appointment of arbitrators.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: So, the process that we have designed in this, is in terms of philosophy, aligned with that of leading institutions around the world.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: In similar fashion, the appointing authority will appoint the third arbitrator upon the request of any party, and if the two arbitrators appointed by the parties fail to agree on the appointment of the third arbitrator within the timeframe specified.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Again, the appointing authority is granted discretion to consider all relevant circumstances, in coming to its decision.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: And these may also include the reasons why the two appointed arbitrators are not able to agree on the third arbitrator or their reasons for failing to come to an agreement within a specified time.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Introducing this default mode of appointment in multi-party arbitrations will reduce potential delay in the conduct of arbitration proceedings.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: And this might arise where parties are unable to agree or refuse to agree as I mentioned earlier.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Or, if the party-appointed arbitrators are themselves, unable to agree on a third appointment.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: As any party in this default mode of appointment would have the right to make a request to the appointing authority, to cite reasons and to request the authority to make the appointment.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: This would also, as I mentioned, avoid the problem of parties seeking to delay or frustrate the arbitration by not taking part in the process at all.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: And we believe that ultimately, this default mechanism, that is set up upfront, will save time for parties, will increase the overall efficiency of the process and will be a further step in continuing to make Singapore an attractive seat for complex international arbitration disputes including those with include multi-parties.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Currently, unless parties otherwise agree, the parties and the arbitral tribunal have a duty of confidentiality.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: This can arise in a number of ways.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: First, as a result of an agreement between the parties.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Second, under any written law or rule of law and this includes the common law.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Third, under the rules of arbitration including the rules of arbitration of an institution or organisation, which the parties have agreed to, or have been adopted by the parties.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Confidential information obtained in anarbitration proceeding is protected from disclosure or use for any other collateral purpose, not the purposes for which the information was obtained, which is the arbitration.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: The scope and content of such a duty might differ.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: In other words, what does this duty cover, what kind of information, what type of documents?

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: And depending on the circumstances of each case, this duty could cover documents used or disclosed in the proceedings.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Our Courts over several decided cases have recognised that, in the absence of an express agreement between the parties regarding the existence and the scope of a duty of confidentiality, even in that parties to the arbitration have an implied duty of confidentiality.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: At the same time, our courts have also commented that there ought not be any generalisations as to what the duty of confidentiality would encompass.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: In other words, do not set out upfront for every case and in each and every case for each type of categories of documents, what that scope of confidentiality covers because each case ought to be evaluated and contextualised in its own circumstances and the implied duty reflects the needs and expectations of the parties as well.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: A distinction has to be drawn between different types of confidentiality attaching to different types of documents or evidence that has been obtained in these proceedings.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: So, for example, arbitration awards may be treated differently from the underlying materials used or disclosed in the course of arbitration proceedings.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: This duty is also not absolute and the extent to which the duty is preserved will depend on the individual circumstances.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Given the centrality of confidentiality in arbitration, parties expect that their various obligations of confidentiality can be protected.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: However, the International Arbitration Act, as it currently stands, does not expressly recognise that.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: The arbitral tribunal does not recognise that the arbitral tribunal or the Courts have the power to enforce existing confidentiality obligations in the event of any such breach.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: These powers will apply, regardless of whether the obligations arise under any of the limbs which I mentioned earlier, whether the obligation arises by written law, by rule of law, under common law, rules of arbitration or by agreement between parties.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: The amendment recognises that confidentiality is an important attribute of arbitration and that the common law is still developing as to the precise extent of the obligation, in other words, whom it should bind and the exceptions, if any, to the rules.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: It does not impose any new or additional obligations of parties beyond what has been set out in those three broad categories that I have mentioned.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: It will also show the international arbitration community that we have a continued commitment to providing strong legislative support for international arbitration.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: I rise in support of this Bill, which amends the International Arbitration Act or IAA and seeks to enhance Singapore’s status as an international commercial arbitration hub.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Over the years, Singapore’s position as an international dispute resolution hub in the globe has been cemented, largely due to its strong recognition of the rule of law.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Alternative dispute resolution mechanisms – in particular, mediation and arbitration, are increasingly popular in recent times, with the privacy afforded to parties at such forums.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Additionally, the Singapore Courts have also recognised arbitration agreements and stayed Court proceedings commenced in breach of such agreements.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: I welcome the amendments, for the following reasons.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: In an era where contractual obligations are being restructured, varied, suspended and/or terminated, as a result of the unprecedented impact of COVID-19 on global economies, the potential for disputes over substantive matters is rife.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: The complexity of such matters may be exacerbated where there are more than two parties involved in the dispute.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: We note that there is a growing trend in arbitrations from joint ventures, oil and gas matters, and merger and acquisition disputes – these disputes often involve substantial sums of monies, and there is all the more reason why we want these matters to be arbitrated in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Additionally, privacy and confidentiality remain the cornerstone of arbitration.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: While the amendments do not seek to impose fresh and/or new confidentiality obligations in arbitration proceedings, my query relates to the scope of such existing obligations.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: The authorities suggest that the general principle in Singapore’s arbitration law is that arbitrations are not only private but also confidential.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: The High Court in Myanma Yaung Chi Oo Co Ltd v Win Win Nu and another in 2003 held that “there was an implied obligation on the parties obtaining documents not to disclose them or use them for any purpose other than the dispute in which they were obtained.” Disclosure, however, may be permissible in certain circumstances, such as the consent of the other party; by order or leave of Court; where it is reasonably necessary; and/or where it was in the interests of justice or where legally required.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Would the Minister be able to provide certain specific instances in which confidentiality obligations are waived?

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: For instance, where documents and/or evidence are raised in arbitration proceedings for which a finding has been made, are subsequently raised in court proceedings for a separate matter between the same parties who wish to deviate from their original position?

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: I declare my interest as a dispute resolution lawyer who practises international arbitration.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Between June and August last year, MinLaw proposed several amendments to the International Arbitration Act for public consultations.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Generally, when an agreement is entered into parties would usually include standard arbitration clauses in those agreements.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: These clauses would typically provide for tribunals consisting of a sole arbitrator, or sometimes three arbitrators.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Where there are three arbitrators to be appointed, the usual method is for the Claimant to appoint one, the Respondent to appoint one and for the two appointed arbitrators to agree on a third.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: These are general practices, of course, specific clauses may vary.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: If the two party appointed arbitrators cannot agree on the third, namely that it will be appointed by some third party, usually institution appointed under the arbitration agreement.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Where problems arise is if there are more than two adverse parties in an arbitration and all are separately represented.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: I think the Minister highlighted several examples in his speech.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: And this is increasingly common in the context of multi-party agreements or in a situation where different agreements are consolidated because we now have rules permitting consolidation of arbitrations.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: So, in this scenario where you have three parties or more, there is a greater likelihood that parties will not be able to agree upon "party appointed" arbitrators.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: For example, if there are multiple Respondents, each separately represented and with different views on the same issue, there may be deadlock.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: What these rules provide for is the default appointment of arbitrators in such situations, which is eminently sensible.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: It requires parties to name arbitrators at specific points in the process as well.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: So, this also reduces the chance that the appointment of arbitrators will be used as a way to delay proceedings.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Now, the core of arbitration is always party autonomy and party autonomy is still protected here because if parties have agreed on their own default mechanism where agreement cannot be reached, that should still prevail.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: What this amendment deals with such a situation where parties did not really provide the mechanism but would not have wanted deadlock either.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: So, what this provides is really a process by which this deadlock can be broken and the arbitration process can be moved smoothly along, even where parties or whether there are three or more parties who cannot agree on the arbitrator.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: This is also one of the main attractions of arbitration for many parties as they would prefer to settle disputes out of the public eye.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: However, the protection of confidentiality is sometimes more difficult because the most common remedy for breach of confidentiality is to get an injunction to prevent dissemination of the information.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: This would only be available if the information is not already in the public domain.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Thus, speed is of the essence if one wishes to get injunctive relief to protect confidentiality of matters subject to arbitration.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: For most practitioners, we would agree that the Tribunal always have powers to make such orders but this was never expressly set out in the legislation.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Of course, the scope of this obligation is not defined precisely but this is necessary because exactly what documents are covered by it, which are already out in the public domain, which are not – these are all matters for that Tribunal to decide.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: But at least the one debate that will be off the table is whether or not the Tribunal has these powers.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: The other benefit of putting it in this section of the International Arbitration Act is that the Court will also now have the power to make an order where a Tribunal is not able to so this is also, I think, necessary as a catch all provision because given the speed with which one has to move if you want to protect confidentiality.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: If the Tribunal is not in place, for example, it may be necessary to go to the Courts to get such an order.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: I support and welcome both of these amendments.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: I think they both solve practical problems that practitioners encounter and it is a tidy solution.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: I would also add, in my concluding remarks, that I also agree with the other four proposals the Ministry had put forward in the consultation and hope that these too can be implemented in due course.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Each of these are good solutions to practical problems.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: I declare my interest as a legal practitioner in international arbitration disputes.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: The two broad areas of amendments that the Bill proposes in relation to multi-party arbitration and powers of arbitral tribunals and the High Court are important are important and very much welcome.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: These amendments are also timely since the last amendments came in 2012.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: I have no doubt that with these amendments, more parties will benefit by bringing their disputes seated in Singapore or before the Singapore International Arbitration Centre or SIAC.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: There were various proposals stated in the public consultation paper.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: It has to be noted, though, that since the conclusion of the public consultation in 2019, admittedly we are now facing a much-changed global legal landscape ravaged by the current COVID-19 pandemic.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Since the pandemic, there has been an uptick in terms of brewing cross-border disputes arising out of force majeure, impossibility of performance and other contractual breaches.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: However, even with our Singapore law firms’ increasing global presence, connections and international expertise, we continually face stiff competition to attract these disputes to our shores.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: This is because clients and litigants are not only more sophisticated, but they are more sensitive to disputes, especially during this time.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: They are craving for certainty both in terms of costs and outcome of arbitration proceedings especially in the midst of this economic outlook.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: They require more flexibility; some may prefer greater court supervision on matters of law in arbitral proceedings.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Others, as so, and prefer to waive appeals to the High Court on arbitral awards in the interests of having finality in the arbitral process.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: My focus is on two separate proposals raised in the consultation paper which are not tabled here in this Bill.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: I believe that these proposals would be beneficial to Singapore.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Parties would have more options and flexibility to tailor an international agreement to suit their unique purposes, especially in preparation for a post-COVID world.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: This would hopefully then attract more cross-border transactions and international disputes to be heard before the Singapore Courts and SIAC.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Consequently, it would only mean more exposure and training for our local lawyers from a professional development standpoint.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: As an international disputes lawyer, I have handled disputes in various jurisdictions and arbitration centres, SIAC here, London Court of International Arbitration and International Court of Arbitration in London and Paris.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: However, looking at the current climate, local younger lawyers, may not get much exposure and opportunity to experience handling international arbitration disputes.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: As such, we need to consider tabling these other proposals soon for the benefit of our future generations of talent.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: But I fear that if we do not fill the glass up now, we may be too late to do so in the future.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Clarifications notwithstanding, Mr Speaker, I support the amendments to the Bill.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The amendments in this Bill will further strengthen our international arbitration regime and raise Singapore’s profile as a global centre for international arbitration.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Parties who require arbitration services will also have access to a wider range of options best tailored to their needs.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: That said, I have a few clarifications on the Bill, many of which, Minister Edwin has already clarified on.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: My first clarification is on the default mode of appointment of arbitrators in multi-party arbitration.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: It is good that we recognise that we need to provide for the appointment of arbitrators in multi-party disputes which are on the rise.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: They occur, for instance, in disputes involving joint ventures, mergers and oil and gas acquisition.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The authority can also reappoint or revoke any appointments made.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: It is unclear why the failure of just one side to appoint an arbitrator means that the appointing authority must now step in to appoint all three arbitrators even if the other side managed to agree on their arbitrator.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Essentially, this means that failure to agree by one side, makes the agreement reached by the other side ineffective.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I do understand that it is common for arbitration institutions to require the appointing authority to appoint all three arbitrators if either the claimants or the respondents are unable to come to an agreement on an arbitrator.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: However, there is a permutation on this model under article 8(1) of the 2020 London Court of International Arbitration Rules.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: It says: where all parties have agreed in writing for each side to nominate a single arbitrator, but one side is not able to come to an agreement on a nomination, the other side is free to make its nomination.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Party autonomy is a significant feature of arbitration.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: To ensure that parties’ agreements are given consideration, can the Minister confirm that the appointing authority should take into account the agreement reached by parties on one side on their arbitrator when appointing the three arbitrators?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: My second clarification is on the amendment to expressly recognise the powers of the arbitral tribunal and the High Court to enforce obligations of confidentiality.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: This amendment is welcome and will assist in tightening the process and preserving confidentiality of the proceedings.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: That said, despite the express recognition, the Bill does not codify confidentiality obligations that the Minister mentioned.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Given that one of the main draws of arbitration is the confidentiality of proceedings, and codifying confidentiality obligations will assist in reducing uncertainty and potential disputes over these obligations, can the Minister clarify the reasoning behind deciding against codifying confidentiality obligations?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: For a good example, we can take a look at the arbitration scene in Hong Kong.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Under section 18(1) of the Arbitration Ordinance, unless agreed by the parties, no party may publish, disclose or communicate information relating to the arbitral proceedings and awards.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Notably, this confidentiality extends to the existence of arbitration proceedings.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: This position is also mirrored in article 45.1 of the 2018 Hong Kong International Arbitration Centre Rules.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Hong Kong was ranked among the top five seats of arbitration worldwide in 2018 and still continues to have a lead over our own SIAC in 2019.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: We note that codifying confidentiality obligations may lead to some challenges.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: For instance, there may be difficulties in defining the scope of the duty of confidentiality and its exceptions.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: However, such difficulties are already present in our current approach of implying the duty of confidentiality in arbitration.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: In fact, it is not uncommon for arbitration proceedings to be delayed because of parties disputing over their scope of implied duty of confidentiality.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The delay reduces one of the main draws of arbitration – its efficiency.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I hope the Minister will consider codifying confidentiality obligations, whether in the Act itself or in subsidiary legislation, as this would encourage parties to arbitrate in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: My final clarification is on the exclusion of the proposed opt-in mechanism for parties to incorporate a right to appeal to the High Court, on a question of law arising out of an arbitral award.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: As things stand, parties may only apply to the High Court to set aside an arbitral award on relatively limited grounds.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: These grounds include fraud, corruption, breach of the rules of natural justice or contravention of Singapore’s public policy.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: One of the key components of arbitration proceedings is finality.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: However, this should not be at the expense of leaving questions of law unresolved.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: This may potentially have significant impact on the substantive rights of parties.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: In fact, the right to appeal on a question of law has already been expressly recognised in our domestic arbitration.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: If I may add, Sir, I slowed down my speech and spaced it out significantly so that I did not deliver my speech in a quick-fire fashion as Minister Edwin mentioned at the last Sitting about my speeches.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I took into account the Minister’s previous feedback and I hope that he will now agree to all my proposals in this speech.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: And obviously, our whole eco-system in encouraging parties to come into Singapore and choose Singapore as a neutral, trusted venue.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: We understand and agree with this principle which really undergirds the amendments that we have proposed in this Bill.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Members have sought various clarifications and I will address these in turn.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Mr Ng’s first question relates to the question of whether the appointing authority should also take into account the agreement that had already been reached by the parties at the stage where the appointing party’s role is triggered, and whether it should take that into account when deciding on the appointment all three arbitrators.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: In the feedback we that we received from the various consultations, the principle of equal treatment of the parties in the context especially of the appointment of the tribunal was something which was emphasised to us.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Arbitral institutional rules and also the national laws unanimously impose a requirement, whether express or implied, that the parties be treated equally throughout the process.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: In other words, the moment there is a disagreement on one party's nomination, then the rules either permit or, in fact, they require the appointing authority to designate the entire tribunal.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: That is the position in LCIA and also some other major institutions.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The reason behind this is to preclude imbalance or, at least, the perception of imbalance in the way in which the tribunal is subsequently appointed and avoid a situation where just one party has a say on his or her nominee for the arbitration.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: In scoping section 9B, we can see that there are many reasons why a party may not be able to agree or has chosen not to agree to the arbitrator.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: It could be because parties do not identify with the same “side” as the party nominating it even though we may be co-respondents to the arbitration, or it may be because one party is intentionally delaying the proceedings, not nominating, or dragging its feet, as I have mentioned earlier, so as to trigger the default mechanism to appoint all three and, in that process, hope to sideline the choice put up by the other party.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: So, to that extent, the authority can look at factors, such as whether the parties on one side may have reached an agreement or not in the way that Mr Louis Ng has put it, or the reasons why one side was not able to come to an agreement.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: It may not be because of trying to frustrate the process or trying to delay the proceedings.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: And the appointing authority will have the ability to look at and study all these factors.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: We believe that this strikes the right balance between the principles of equality and also party autonomy, something that Mr Louis Ng and Mr Vikram Nair also spoke about.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The amendments do not seek to change the law or add new obligations, but seeks to ensure that it is clear beyond the pale that the tribunal and the High Court will have the power to enforce these obligations.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Mr Patrick Tay asked for clarifications on instances where the obligations might be waived.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: As Mr Patrick Tay mentioned, Justice Kan mentioned this in a 2003 decision that it is implied that parties who choose arbitration are more likely to take into account the fact that these are private hearings and have the cloak of confidentiality.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The Courts, however, have also noted – and I think Mr Patrick Tay also briefly alluded to that – that we should take care not to generalise what that duty would encompass upfront, that is, not to spell it out upfront.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Mr Vikram Nair also noted that this gives a degree of flexibility because, as a case proceeds, the quality and nature of confidentiality over a specific piece of information or document might change.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Likewise, whether or when a confidentiality obligation is to be waived must also be assessed in the context of the facts in which the issue arises.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: I would add that, in any given case, regard must also be given to the chosen institutional rules that the parties have agreed will apply to their own arbitration and whether or not there are any specific rules in that setting relevant to the way in which they look at confidentiality.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: I will come back to this point in a moment as I address Mr Louis Ng's other point in a less quick-fire way.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Moving to Mr Louis Ng's question as to why the obligation of confidentiality is not codified and whether we would consider doing so, let me again give a bit of background.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: As I have mentioned earlier, it has its roots in common law, so it is implied in the proceedings.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Mr Louis Ng mentioned that, in Hong Kong, it has been codified and it might then improve or, at least, enhance the proceedings.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: So, what Hong Kong has done is to say that there is a duty of confidentiality.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: But in our proceedings here in Singapore, especially in the context of what I have mentioned in the SIAC Rules, it is really quite unarguable.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: What the real issue is, when it comes to confidentiality, is often what are the quality and nature of that confidentiality.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: What does it do to the information and documents that are exchanged in those proceedings?

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: That, as I have mentioned earlier, might take a different shape or be differently contoured, depending on the context.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Does it apply only to the parties or the witnesses?

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: You may have to look at what are the facts of that case, bring them up and the context, before you assess that question.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: But it may not have the same quality as the start if, subsequently, information is disclosed or allowed to be disclosed or divulged by one party.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: So, the further context as to when you are looking at the issue will also be relevant.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Of course, finally, how is it best enforced?

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Is it by way of an injunction of some sort, a mandatory injunction, or would the parties be allowed to disclose it in a measured way under a ringfence or redacted.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: So, these are all questions that I hope Mr Louis Ng will appreciate, but which arise maybe as a consequence of there being a confidentiality obligation in the first place which, as far as we are concerned, there is no argument over.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Which is why we are proposing these amendments to allow the tribunal and the High Court to enforce these obligations.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: But the question as to what you do with the confidential obligations, how you enforce, is something that ought to be looked at case to case and context to context.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: In addition, we have also taken this view because it is also a recognition that this area of law is still evolving.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: There have been cases, both locally as well as internationally.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Some, Mr Patrick Tay has cited earlier, and also International case law on this and it is a question that is best left to the common law at this stage to develop more fully.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: I would add to Mr Louis Ng's point also that where parties to an agreement – if you come to an agreement and you have a specific concern, you have a specific confidentiality attached to, say, an IP patent or to a piece of information that is very sensitive – it is open to the parties to expressly incorporate provisions specific to their own needs in their arbitration agreement and that will be enforced.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Members will remember that, at the outset, I mentioned that the confidentiality arises in a number of ways, one of which is through the parties' express agreement in the arbitration agreement itself.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Mr Louis Ng will know that the Courts have consistently looked at the scope of the arbitration agreement and to study that to assess the extent of the confidentiality obligations.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Next, let me move on to the amendments which have considered in the consultation but not brought in this Bill.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Both Mr Louis Ng and Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim have enquired about these amendments and the proposals that were considered.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: I think Mr Louis Ng also said that these would add value to our landscape.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: When we are ready with that, we will come back and I am sure we will also consult with Mr Louis Ng and the others who have raised the points here.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: In the final analysis, on these points, I want to assure Members and the arbitration community that my Ministry recognises the range of options and the diversity of views on these proposals.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: As I have said, some go towards whether or not they should be implemented; others have given us suggestions as to how they can be implemented.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: As I have flagged, this is a process that is on-going and we are always taking into account what users want to see – developments in the law and, of course, international conventions and practices as well.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: We will continue to make Singapore an attractive seat for arbitration disputes.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: With that, Sir, I beg to move.      .
